title: Re: Control legacy Fender Mustang amps from the browse...
text:
I created ReFUSE to bring my old Fender Mustang (from 2013) modelling amplifier back to life.

The amplifier itself still sounds great, especially for home practise, but the official Fender FUSE control software was discontinued years ago. The software let you configure the amp models and effects, their parameters etc, which aren't not accessible from the physical knobs on the amplifier itself. And because it was originally built on Microsoft Silverlight, it became completely unusable on modern operating systems.

So, instead of letting this amp slowly turn into e-waste, I built an Angular web client using the browser's WebHID API. To start, I relied heavily on prior reverse engineering work and documentation from similar FUSE projects GitHub. Further debugging of the protocol was done in collaboration with Gemini, helping to understand the packet structure and quirks. Me twisting knobs on the amp, and AI analyzing the data stream and finding patterns was fascinating.

I had lots of fun building this, and because of the close collab with AI, I was able to write this complicated application, and fancy illustrations, in only a couple of evenings and those moments when while my 2yo daughter was taking the naps.

If you have a Fender Mustang amplifier lying around, please give it a try and share your thoughts!

title: Show HN: Clawdline – Manage Claude Code/Codex sessions across computers
text:
I built Clawdline to manage Claude Code and Codex sessions across multiple computers in one place.

It runs on multiple computers (Mac and Linux), and you can see all of your sessions in one list. Each session reports its status (working, completed, or needs attention). You can also manage all your sessions and receive notifications from your phone (web app).

Herdr, T3 Code, and Orca already cover a lot of this space, and there’s overlap.

When I started building Clawdline, I didn't know about Herdr, T3 Code, or Orca. So I built it to fit my own dev workflow. At first, I used Swift to build a Mac app, but I realized that it wouldn't work if I also wanted to support Linux. So I decided to rewrite it in Go. Now it can support both of them.

Main Features:

- Cross Machine Agent Communication: You can ask a root session ("Local") on your Mac to start a new session ("Remote") on a remote Linux machine. Once the remote session finishes its work, it notifies the root ("Local") session.

- Cross Agent Communication: You can use one root session to create tasks need multiple agents. They can communicate with each other through clawdline

- Scheduled Task with Webhook: You can create scheduled tasks and combine them with your service (use webhooks to trigger new agent sessions)

- Board System: tasks control for Feature, Issue, Epic, Refactor, Plan

- Snippet/Playbook: If there are commands you use them very often, snippet can help you

- TODO: lightweight tasks

- Note: Agents can leave notes to you if they need your attention

- Agent Squad: assign role to any task or session

- Archive: you can archive sessions and see it in one place

- Others: Intelligence session naming, Image/Video display, Voice input, Machine monitor, Usage Monitor, Dev Stack Run, Deploy progress monitor...

This project is open source and I have used Claude & Codex to do independent reviews on Clawdline, Herdr, T3 and Orca. (you can find the reviews on the website.)

The work still needs further input and feedback. Hope this helps other developers improve their devs! :)

title: Re: Ask HN: Will apps be going away in favor of person...
text:
I think a chatbot or voice is a horrible interface for most things. There is 0 chance for discoverability, so the application's function is limited by the user's imagination. Most people aren't going to think about the various things a program could solve for them. Even with a UI, most users only use a small fraction of the available options. Without some visual cue to let them know features exist, I'd bet that most users would use even less.

My day job is automation stuff within a large organization. Most people, even within a technical organization, don't seem to think about how the computer can solve problems for them. The other day I used Claude to turn a massive csv dump of data into a dashboard to see trends over time. I don't see other people doing that.. but if Excel had a button for it, I'm sure they would do it.

title: Re: Jepsen: ParticleDB 1.1.4...
text:
I’ve come to learn an interesting dichotomy in software:

Some software is correct by construction, in the sense that the overall design makes sense and the cases that don’t work are generally local bugs.

Some software is incorrect by construction, and it tends to work by some combination of luck and by carefully working around the incorrect design in most or all code paths that could expose the incorrectness. (AI can be quite effective at finding the relevant places to insert workarounds.)

ParticleDB sounds like the latter category. Plenty of large projects have portions that are in one category and portions that are in another.

As an aside, for the last day or two, I’ve been contemplating that the Linux kernel’s handling of folio pinning seems to be in the incorrect-by-construction category. Good times. No, I haven’t found a hard-to-fix bug that I would credibly characterize as a security or likely accidental corruption issue [0], but this seems mostly like luck.

[0] I do appear to have re-discovered a bug that some massive Anthropic dump from a couple months ago also found, and it’s getting fixed. If your application does “fixed” io_uring I/O or certain types of iommu-based or maybe RDMA on a memfd, you might plausibly encounter it on rare occasions. I didn’t bother making a reproducer.

title: Re: Prospero: A new coding harness for a more civilize...
text:
Nice to see a gui coding agent. I use tui agents all the time but I am building a gui one. I use Claude Code, Codex, opencode and a couple other but I do not like the DX/UX.

I often want click a part of the wall of text (from agent) and search for related text, open them up on the side or so. I want to open a linked file. I want to answer multiple questions in an async manner, even come back and continue answering the next day.

There are many prompt level features I want too - orchestrate with subagents, but only the tasks I select - how do I select when there is no checkbox. Or maybe delegate a subagent to dig into (read only) one portion of the chat response. Maybe codify (write) only one task in a list of tasks. So many many other small things.

As a full-time user of coding agents, the TUI barely works for me. I think splitting text, searching in text, merging text are more important in agent driven development than ever before. It is all text, all the way. This is what I am building myself, with my own gui framework.

text: Something about the writing style here makes it hard for me to follow what actually happened. The section about JSONP for example seems to be explaining how JSONP works and how it's designed as an attempt to work around these attacks, but that explanation is then passed off as an explanation of how they bypassed the protection. And the whole premise seems to be about how manipulating the Preview content let them work through multiple defensive layers, but I don't see an explanation of how they directly controlled that content in the first place. title: Why Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI need their own AI detection tools
text:
I'm not naive enough to think that these companies don't already have some internal detection tools, but they clearly are not being used enough. Lately researching anything using agents has been a pain (especially if the query leads up to buying intent) - the sources quoted are often AI slop, which are then used to deterministically argue a point. On the first challenge to logic, the reply is usually an apology followed by a tangential search and agreement on the user argued point - sometimes even a hedge. There is a simple problem embedded at the center of this, that at least partially explains this degradation - AI generated text. There is now arguably more AI generated text on the web than human writings, and platforms that used to be very credible (attracting high quality technical writers) now seem to be full of AI generated slop (someone has to call them out). It's a pattern I'm sure most people are noticing under the hood - query -> beautiful prose -> suspect sources. You challenge the answer, and all of a sudden it's a wildly different conclusion. To me that just sounds unreliable, because you could potentially argue with it to generate any conclusion you want - doesn't sound like a reliable brainstorming partner anymore. Not to mention it's preference for believing structured AI prose output as high quality writing. Perhaps it is simply a byproduct of the baked in agreeability or "dooms-day" protections baked in to system prompts. This makes it even more important to have sources quoted by bots verified for authority and origin. The authority test is being easily faked by rampant SEO abuse on once reliable blogging platforms (I won't name them but you know who) - apparently one bot - sorry user - singing product praises is enough for chat to recommend that product, mind-boggling. And one biased - sorry tailored - article comparing a product to 5 competitors is enough to determine which is best. If this is not a crisis, idk what is.

The detection problem: Using conventional techniques like duplicate detection, repetition and similarity filters on AI generated content is a lost cause - there's enough probabilistic variance in them to generate millions of different copies.

One solution to the problem: Use an AI detector to adjust result ranks. By adjusting the ranking using AI generated labels, not only will engines prioritise genuine human writings - they also potentially refer to a wider range of opinions on a subject, improving diversity consulted in answers. I know it sounds like an over-simplification, and it probably is - but to me it does sound like a first step in the right direction.

Taken from https://t9xt.com/writings/why-google-microsoft-anthropic-and-openai-need-to-build-their-own-ai-detection-tools-before-it-i

title: Tell HN: Claude is using my limits even though it's infra is failing
text:
I am using Claude design, and a lot of times it's agent is failing mid-task, with connection errors (not sure is this connection between me and agent, or between agent in Claude infra and relevant LLM model)

When these errors happen:

1. My limits have been consumed already

2. There is no resume button, there is only retry, which starts again

3. Even retry fails, then consumes my tokens.

I had some chats where I lost 80% my limits by retrying the task, with no luck of completing it.
